The authors' design rule is to design for intended use and also for the kinds of new uses the firm is willing to seed and commercialize. ### Generative AI in the Front End: Effort Saved Is Not Creativity Gained {#sec-innovation-genai-ideation} The front end of the funnel above is where generative AI has been adopted fastest, on the reasoning that turning a vague idea into a developed concept is laborious and the labor can be offloaded. @gordetzki2026ideation test that reasoning and find it backwards in an instructive way. In an online experiment, 276 participants refined ideas for an innovation challenge either alone, with AI-generated *text*, or with AI-generated *images*. Image-based support did what it was supposed to do on the effort margin: it significantly reduced effort relative to both working alone and text-based support. It also produced ideas that were **18% less creative** than those from the more effortful text-based support. The explanation is about what each format leaves undone. An image specifies every detail of a concept, and a fully specified concept leaves the human nothing to complete. Text leaves gaps, and filling gaps is effortful precisely because it is generative. The effect is moderated by how far the idea has already been developed: textual input helps most when the concept is already mature, because there is enough structure for the human's completions to attach to. The result should be read as a claim about **agency configuration** rather than about model quality—the question is how much of the concretization work the tool takes over, not how good the tool is. That reframing matters for NPD practice because it makes the design variable something a manager controls. It also supplies a caution for the measurement discussion in @sec-innovation-measure: an ideation tool evaluated on throughput or on time-to-concept will score the image condition best, and an evaluation restricted to those metrics would recommend exactly the configuration that degrades the output the process exists to produce. ### Quality Without Variety: The Diversity Cost of LLM Ideation {#sec-innovation-llm-diversity} The companion question is what happens when the model is asked to *generate* the ideas rather than help concretize them, and there the accounting runs the other way: the per-idea numbers look excellent and the portfolio numbers do not. @terwiesch2026creativity run eight studies on one tightly bounded ideation task—a new physical product for the U.S. college-student market retailing under \$50—chosen because it is the challenge format long used in product-design courses, so a large pool of pre-LLM human ideas exists for comparison. Idea quality is measured as this literature has long measured it: average **purchase intent** elicited from target-market consumers, the best available single-number predictor of an idea's eventual value. On that metric the LLM wins outright. LLM-generated ideas have higher average quality than human ideas and are **seven times more likely** to land in the pooled top decile, and a second study rules out the obvious deflationary explanation—that the model is merely writing better sales copy around equally good ideas. The weakness appears only when the unit of analysis moves from the idea to the *set*: AI ideas are less novel individually and, more consequentially, less **diverse** collectively. A fifth study re-analyzes prior LLM creativity experiments and finds the same diversity shortfall in every one, which upgrades the result from an artifact of one prompt to a property of the generator. That ordering—quality up, diversity down—matters more than either finding alone because of what an idea pool is *for*. A tournament does not consume the mean of its pool; it consumes the maximum, and the expected maximum of a sample rises with dispersion as well as with location. A generator that shifts the quality distribution rightward while compressing its spread, and while concentrating the draws in one region of the idea space, can dominate on every per-idea metric and still yield a worse best idea, because the search has been narrowed. The measurement lesson is the one @sec-innovation-creativity-embeddings makes with patent text: novelty and diversity are *set-level* quantities that no average of item-level scores recovers, so an evaluation reporting only mean purchase intent is structurally blind to the cost being incurred. The remaining studies buy the variance back, and in doing so establish that the shortfall is a configuration problem rather than a hard ceiling. Newer model versions generate more diverse sets than older ones but still fall short of human sets. Three interventions close most of what remains: **pooling** ideas across vendors, so that one model's training idiosyncrasies do not define the search; **prompt engineering**— chain-of-thought, and injecting heterogeneous personas or constraints, each of which pushes the sampler off its modal completion; and **creative agents** instructed to explore the solution landscape deliberately. A final study exploits the economics directly: because the marginal cost of one more AI idea is near zero, simply generating far more of them steadily improves coverage of the idea space and approaches human-level coverage. For an innovation manager the synthesis is that the human pool is less a diversity benchmark to be matched by a cleverer prompt than a coverage target that can be purchased with scale, heterogeneity, or both. Read alongside @gordetzki2026ideation, the two results point at the same design variable from opposite ends of the front end. Concretization support degrades creativity by leaving the human nothing to complete; generation support degrades diversity by leaving the *search* nothing to explore. In both cases the metric that would have caught the problem—effort in one, set-level coverage in the other—is the first one a throughput-oriented evaluation drops. ## Organizational Determinants of Innovation Beyond the project and the boardroom lies the question of which *organizational* arrangements expand or erode a firm's stock of innovative capacity—what several authors call its **innovation base**, the accumulated inventions, ideas, and discoveries that propel future innovation. ### Acquisitions and the Innovation Base The evidence on whether acquisitions help or harm innovation is genuinely mixed, and the resolution is conditional. @hitt1991 document a *negative* average effect: acquisition activity reduces R&D inputs and outputs, including patent counts, as managerial attention and capital are absorbed by integration. @mishra2013building, analyzing 352 firms across five industries over seventeen years, qualify this: firms that acquire build a *more* robust innovation base than those that do not, but the benefit depends on the **type** of acquisition—vertical (across supply-chain stages) versus horizontal (same stage, similar chains)—and, critically, on the **breadth of knowledge** in the acquiring firm, which determines whether either acquisition type actually enriches the base. @king2008performance reconcile the two by emphasizing **resource interactions**: acquisitions raise performance only when target and acquirer resources are *complementary*. Marketing–technology complementarity (strong-marketing acquirer, strong-technology target) creates value, whereas technology–technology overlap is substitutive and can destroy it. The apparent contradiction in the literature thus dissolves into a moderation structure—average effects are uninformative when complementarity varies across deals. ### Firm Boundaries: Franchising and External Knowledge Firms also reshape their innovation capacity by reconfiguring their boundaries. @mallapragada2017innovativeness study **franchising** as such a lever, using panel data on 38 U.S. restaurant chains (1992–2005) and a nonlinear seemingly-unrelated- regression model. They find a positive relationship between franchising emphasis and *product* innovativeness that intensifies under high financial leverage and weakens under high slack resources, with a parallel but distinctly moderated pattern for *process* innovativeness. Franchising, on this evidence, is a conditional substitute for alliances and joint ventures in shaping innovation outcomes. Knowledge also enters the firm through less formal channels. @baruffaldi2024like show that firms learn at **scientific conferences**, especially when they engage intensely through both sponsorship and scientific contribution. Using direct flights as an instrumental variable for attendance—an instrument that shifts the cost of attending without plausibly affecting innovation through other channels—they find that co-attendance with other scientists raises the likelihood of leveraging external knowledge and of future collaboration, with learning skewed toward prominent firms and scientists. The instrument is what makes the learning claim *causal* rather than merely correlational: firms that attend more conferences differ in unobservable ways from those that do not, and direct flights break that confound. ### Who You Know in the Lab: Networks and Absorptive Capacity {#sec-innovation-academic-networks} Conferences are a scheduled, purchasable channel. @arts2026harnessing ask about the unscheduled one, and open with a puzzle the chapter's measurement section has already half-stated: firms conduct less scientific research internally than they once did, yet their patents lean *more* heavily on science. If the science is not being made in house, how does it get in? The public-good answer is that it does not need a channel— published findings are there for anyone to read, and a firm's problem is only whether it is looking. The authors' answer is that reading is not the binding constraint. They construct a social network covering nearly the entire population of life-science academic scientists and corporate inventors listed on U.S. patents, then confront the selection problem that has dogged every prior attempt at this question. A firm that cites a professor's paper may do so because it knows the professor, or because the paper was the best and most commercializable science available—and the two are correlated, because good scientists attract both citations and connections. The design that breaks the tie is **paper twins**: pairs of scientific papers reporting nearly identical findings, published at nearly the same time, by independent academic teams. Within a twin pair the knowledge itself is held fixed, along with its timing and its commercial potential; what differs is which team the firm's inventors happen to be connected to. Comparing which twin a corporate patent cites is therefore a comparison of social distance with content controlled, the same maneuver as a matched-pairs experiment and the reason the estimate can be read as transmission rather than quality (@sec-graph-identification). Connections win. Academic science travels into corporate patents along *close* interpersonal ties—within two degrees of separation—so the twin whose authors sit a coauthor, or a coauthor's coauthor, away from the inventor is the one that gets cited. Two degrees is a short reach in a network of that size, and the shortness is the substantive result: this is not diffuse network embeddedness paying off, it is knowing someone, or knowing someone who does. Science may be a public good in the sense that no one is excluded from reading it, but absorbing it is rival, and the rationing device is the social graph. The moderators are where the paper meets this chapter's recurring theme. The value of a connection depends on the corporate inventor's own active engagement in scientific research, and on the alignment between that inventor's scientific expertise and the academic knowledge being integrated. A tie into a laboratory is worth little to an inventor who has stopped doing science, or whose expertise lies elsewhere. That is **absorptive capacity** recovered at the level of the individual inventor rather than the firm, and it is the same conditional structure as the acquisition results above and the open-source results below: external knowledge is not an average effect but a complementarity, and internal research capability is the organ that digests it. It also sharpens how the science-linkage measures of @sec-innovation-measure should be read. A firm's count of patent citations to scientific papers is usually taken as a measure of how science-intensive its technology is; on this evidence it is partly a measure of whose calls its inventors can get returned. (INFORMS and SSRN were both inaccessible when this was written; the account above rests on the published abstract.) The same conditional structure appears when the network is inside the firm. @breschi2026ethnic ask how ethnic diversity among a firm's inventors is converted into valuable innovation and argue that composition and collaborative structure are different things. From patent and co-inventor data on 890 publicly traded U.S. firms between 1990 and 2015 they build a network index of ethnic integration, the ratio of cross-ethnic to within-ethnic co-invention ties, and link it to the stock-market reaction around patent grants, the forward-looking value measure that @tbl-citations notes forward citations cannot supply. Integration raises patent value, most in firms that are both ethnically diverse and working on technologically complex innovation, and the estimates survive an instrumental-variables strategy for the endogeneity of collaboration structure. Diversity without integration returns little. (Wiley's site was inaccessible when this was written, so the instrument itself could not be inspected; the account rests on the published abstract.) ### Opening the Boundary: Open-Source Product Development The franchising and conference channels move knowledge *toward* a firm that still owns the development process. **Open-source product development** dissolves that ownership: the firm builds its product in public on a social coding platform such as GitHub, and outside volunteers commit code alongside its own employees. Whether that openness pays is a question about the firm's income statement, not about community goodwill, and @singh2026opensource answer it with a panel of 977 U.S. high-tech firms observed from 2001 to 2025. Firms that adopt open-source product development realize, on average, a **4–5% increase in gross margin**, an estimate that survives staggered difference-in-differences, generalized synthetic control, instrumental-variable, and dynamic-panel specifications (@sec-causal-inference)—four designs with different identifying assumptions converging on the same magnitude, which is what makes the result hard to dismiss as an artifact of any one of them. The interesting content is in the mechanism and its limits. Framing open source as **distributed knowledge integration** in the knowledge-based view of the firm, the authors decompose more than 323,000 project-level contributions across over 44,000 repositories into *internal employee* and *external volunteer* sources, and show that **labor productivity** partially mediates the margin effect: outside expertise enlarges the pool of specialized knowledge applied to the product without a commensurate rise in the wage bill. But the mediated path is not always positive. The indirect effect turns discernibly positive only past a **threshold of roughly 35% external volunteer contribution** (@sec-causal-mediation-firm-panel reads the moderated mediation as a design)—below it, the firm is paying the coordination and review costs of openness without importing enough outside knowledge to cover them. A configurational analysis then adds a second condition: R&D intensity is present in *every* high-profitability configuration, the absorptive capacity required to metabolize externally sourced knowledge (the method is set out in @sec-qual-fsqca, and the three-stage architecture of the paper as a whole in @sec-sw-emb). That is the same conditional logic as the acquisitions literature above, in a different guise—openness, like acquisition, is not an average effect but a complementarity, and a firm without internal R&D has no organ with which to digest what the crowd contributes. Generative AI changes the economics of that crowd. @song2026copilot ask what an AI pair programmer does to open-source development, where participation is voluntary, membership is fluid, and the integration of contributions runs through peer discussion rather than through a manager. GitHub supplied proprietary project-level data on the share of contributors using Copilot, which the authors joined to the public activity records of 9,244 active GitHub projects observed monthly from January 2021, when Copilot entered technical preview, to December 2022, stopping before ChatGPT could contaminate the panel. Treated projects are those in which Copilot was both supported by the contributors' coding environments and actually used; controls are projects whose environments did not support it. Because adoption is staggered and treated projects outnumber controls, the authors estimate a generalized synthetic control (@sec-causal-inference) on the 7,637 projects with at least one contribution, and back it with within-environment comparisons, a matched difference-in-differences, and an instrument built from contributors' exposure to Copilot through their collaborators on other projects. The result is a tradeoff rather than a productivity headline. Copilot use raises merged pull requests per project by 5.9%, and the gain decomposes along both margins that the cost–benefit account of open-source participation predicts: 3.4% more developers with merged code and 2.1% more merged code per developer. But the average time to merge a pull request rises by 8%, and the mechanism is more talk, not less review. Comments per merged request rise 6.5%, distinct commenters 1.7%, and comments per commenter 5.9%, with more topics per discussion and more revision cycles, while core developers complete *more* reviews after adoption, not fewer. The two forces net out positive, with 3.5% to 5.1% more requests merged within one, three, or ten days, and bug and issue counts per merged request are flat, so the extra code is not worse code. The distributional result is the one that matters for the complementarity argument above. The core developers' share of merged code rises by about 5 percentage points (6.5% on a base of 0.83), and the relative time to merge a peripheral contributor's code rises by 5.4%, with peripheral contributions attracting disproportionately more discussion and more requests for context. This is not a skill story: Copilot usage is if anything higher among peripheral developers and their language expertise is comparable. It is a role story. Core developers know the architecture well enough to turn AI-generated suggestions into changes the project can absorb and capture the reputational return on them; peripheral developers, especially new ones, get a lower cost of contributing but not a higher benefit, and their cheaper code costs the project more to integrate. The authors read the pattern as a warning that AI pair programmers may concentrate open-source activity in the core. Read against @singh2026opensource, it is also a warning for firms: if the volunteer share of contribution is what makes openness pay, a tool that tilts contribution toward insiders thins exactly the channel through which external knowledge arrives, and the binding constraint shifts from writing code to coordinating it. ### Inventor Job Security and the Direction of Invention Organizational arrangements shape not only how much a firm invents but *what kind* of invention it gets, and the mechanism can run through a single employment term. The intuitive prediction is that protecting inventors from dismissal buys exploration: an inventor who cannot be fired for a failed project has the safety net that risky, distant search requires. @wehrheim2026paradox test that prediction against the staggered adoption of wrongful-discharge laws across U.S. states between 1980 and 1999, using matched employer–employee data built from patent records and a difference-in-differences design on the cross-state timing. The prediction fails, and the reason is instructive. Job security does not primarily change an inventor's tolerance for failure; it changes the expected length of the relationship, and a longer expected tenure raises the return to investing in *firm-specific* technological knowledge over generally portable knowledge. Under stronger protection, inventors produced patents drawing more heavily on their own firm's technologies, less novel by the backward-citation logic of @sec-innovation-measure, and of higher private value to the employer. The result is a clean case of the private–social wedge that runs through this chapter's measurement discussion. Every outcome improved from the employer's ledger; the novelty of the technological frontier did not. It also sharpens what "organizational determinant" means. The wrongful-discharge laws were labor policy, written about dismissal and evaluated on employment, and their measurable consequence landed on the composition of the patent stock—an untargeted margin of exactly the kind @sec-policy-spillovers is about. A firm that wants exploration from a protected workforce has to buy it with something other than protection, because protection is an incentive to specialize. ### Who Is on the Team and What Gets Made The direction of invention also depends on who is doing the inventing, and a social movement can move it. @luo2026metoo study the early-stage project pipeline in Hollywood around the Harvey Weinstein scandal of October 2017 and the #MeToo movement it set off. The question is about product choice rather than hiring: did production teams change *what* they developed, and did the answer depend on whether the team included a woman? Because #MeToo touched the whole industry, no group was untreated. The authors reuse the device from their earlier study of hiring [@luo2022scandal], which found that producers who had worked with Weinstein became about 35 percent more likely to work with female writers after the scandal, relative to producers who had not. Teams with a past Weinstein collaborator are taken to be treated more intensely, through stigma by association and through the salience of a scandal that involves someone they know. Non-associated teams absorb industry-wide trends such as the 2017 Women's March and Hollywood's broader diversity push. The outcomes come from the logline, the one-to-three-sentence plot summary recorded when a project is set up. One is the protagonist's gender. The other is a BERT-embedding distance that places the protagonist between benchmark vectors built from the masculine and feminine items of the Bem Sex-Role Inventory. On average, the response is zero, and the average hides a split. The working-paper version [@luo2024metoowp] matches 1,977 projects set up between 2014 and 2019, and every estimate below is relative to comparable non-associated teams. All-male Weinstein-associated teams moved toward female-protagonist projects after #MeToo by 11.7 percentage points, an imprecise estimate ($p = 0.19$). Associated teams that included a woman moved the other way, by 15.7 points toward male-protagonist projects. The triple difference between the two responses is 25.8 points ($p = 0.008$). The female protagonists that all-male associated teams developed also moved further from the feminine stereotype than those developed by teams with women. Release outcomes split the same way. Female-protagonist projects from all-male associated teams became 37 points less likely to reach theaters, while associated teams with women released more of their projects whatever the protagonist's gender. The authors read the all-male response as pressure to show progress, which led teams to pick projects that did not fit their capabilities. They read the response of teams with women as entry into a category those teams had found hard to enter. In their data, women wrote only 11 percent of male-protagonist stories, and male-protagonist films had budgets about \$13.8 million higher. The lesson for innovation research is that the gender of the people inventing and the gender of the market they serve are not the same lever. The authors contrast their result with work arguing that more women inventors will mainly mean more products for women. In a category segregated by bias rather than by preference, where skills carry over between male- and female-oriented projects, lowering the barrier shows up first as women moving *out* of the gender-congruent category. A firm that tracks its progress on gender inequality by counting female-oriented products may be measuring the wrong margin. The magnitudes above come from the 2024 working paper; the published abstract reports the same pattern of signs. @luo2026metoo observe the pipeline: what teams chose to develop. Whether those choices reached screens, and how audiences received what did, is the content- and demand-side question that @tran2026metoo take up. Drawing on social role theory and on the framing logic of social movements, they assemble 1,523 top-grossing U.S. films released between 2010 and 2023. For each film they measure portrayals of sexual misconduct, female objectification, and stereotypical and counter-stereotypical gender roles. The measures come from AI-assisted content analysis checked against human coders, supplemented by text analysis of 334,917 crowdsourced movie keywords (@sec-tad-llm-film-coding). There are two findings. First, there is little evidence of meaningful short-run change in the content of released films after #MeToo. Second, audiences penalize films featuring the behaviors the movement targeted, but their preference for traditional gender roles endures. They resist counter-stereotypical portrayals of men and embrace counter-stereotypical portrayals of women only selectively. The University of Arizona's press release puts the stakes of even small differences in these portrayals at \$8 million to \$13 million in box office revenue for a film. A null on content next to a shift in the pipeline is not a contradiction, and the two studies should not be pooled into one verdict on whether #MeToo changed Hollywood. They observe different stages over different horizons (@fig-metoo-stages). The first difference is timing. Cast and plot are settled long before release, at least two and a half years by the estimate used in an earlier version of the study [@tran2023consumerdiss]. Projects set up after October 2017 would therefore mostly reach theaters from 2020 onward, in pandemic-disrupted years at the end of a window that closes in 2023. The second is the counterfactual. Luo and Zhang's estimates are relative to non-associated teams, which absorb industry-wide change by design, while a short-run content change in the sense of Tran, Warren, and Beck is a change in the released slate as a whole. The third is that the pipeline response averaged zero. All-male associated teams moved toward female protagonists while associated teams that included a woman moved away from them, and it was the female-protagonist projects of all-male teams that were less likely to reach theaters. A shift that offsets across teams, and is partly filtered out before release, need not show up in what gets released. That is consistent with Luo and Zhang's finding that the female-protagonist projects of the most pressured teams fared worse, though the two papers do not share a sample and neither tests the link. (Only the published abstract and the university's press release were accessible when this section was written. Neither reports the AI model used, the agreement statistics against human coders, or the box-office specification, so no estimates from the paper are quoted here.) ### Where Inventors Live: Residential Proximity Inside the Firm The organizational arrangements above are all things a firm chooses. @pennington2026residential study one it does not: where its inventors go home at night. The agglomeration literature has long held that geographic proximity between *firms* raises collaboration and knowledge spillovers, and the workplace literature that proximity between *desks* does the same. The authors ask whether the mechanisms behind the second claim—chance encounters, repeated observation, the lowered search and social costs of asking a familiar face for help—operate outside the building, so that two employees of the same facility who live near one another are more likely to end up on the same patent. The setting does much of the identifying work. The orthopedic-implant cluster around Warsaw, Indiana held the research facilities of three of the five largest orthopedic firms in the world (DePuy, Zimmer, and Biomet) within a short drive of one another, with no university, no related industry, and no major city nearby to sort inventors' residences by knowledge type or prior affiliation. Because the firms required inventors to list home addresses in patent-application correspondence, the authors could hand-code residential street addresses from the USPTO Image File Wrapper documents rather than rely on the regional-level addresses in standard patent bibliographies. In the dissertation version of the paper [@pennington2021dissertation], the sample is 1,913 applications filed by the three firms between 2001 and 2015, 702 disambiguated inventors at 752 addresses, and a conditional logit in which every pair of inventors active at the assignee in a five-year window around the filing is a potential coinventor pair on that application (about 122 inventors, hence about 7,400 pairs, per choice set). Each kilometer of distance between two inventors' homes lowers the odds that they appear together on a patent by about 0.3%. A firm whose average pair lived half a standard deviation farther apart would see roughly 5% fewer collaborations per application, and the one firm with the most dispersed inventors was about 17% less collaborative than the other two. The value of the paper is in what it rules out. Homophily is the obvious rival: people who are alike may both live near one another and work together. A shared prior employer or alma mater raises a pair's collaboration odds by about 50% but does not predict how close they live, and it does not attenuate the distance effect when interacted with it; newcomers to the region settle *farther* from people they already know, not closer; differences in block-group household income between the two homes matter on their own but barely dent the proximity coefficient; and the pair's average distance to the town center, where all the R&D facilities sit, is insignificant once pairwise distance is in the model, so it is proximity to each other rather than to work that predicts collaboration. A within-pair test on inventors who moved during the sample period—the same two people, before and after their residential distance changed—recovers an effect of the same sign at about 1% per kilometer with every fixed pair characteristic differenced away. The published version adds that the effect holds for pairs in different product divisions, so residential proximity relaxes an organizational constraint on who collaborates with whom. The one dimension along which proximity does *not* relax a constraint is gender. Same-gender pairs collaborate about 28% more often than mixed-gender pairs, and when distance is interacted with a same-gender indicator the entire proximity effect loads onto same-gender pairs; for mixed-gender pairs, living nearby does nothing. The authors read this as social cost: encounters at the grocery store or the youth sports field escalate into work conversations more readily between two men, or two women, than across genders, so the collaborations that proximity creates are the unplanned ones, and unplanned collaborations inherit the homophily of unplanned social life (@sec-graph-identification). The chapter's recurring lesson about organizational determinants applies with a twist. A geography the firm never designed shapes its patent network, and the same mechanism that adds collaborations subtracts diversity from them. The result is also a caution about *measurement scale* for anyone using location as a variable (@sec-geospatial): a within-commuting-region indicator, the proximity measure most patent studies can afford, would have missed the whole effect, which lives at the resolution of a five-minute versus a ten-minute drive to the same store. The limiting case of proximity without organizational affiliation is the coworking space, where people with different employers, occupations, and goals rent desks in the same room. @hymer2026coworking ask what relationships form there and what value they carry. Applying grounded-theory techniques to observational, archival, and interview data from 80 workers across 21 coworking spaces (@sec-qualitative-research), they arrive at a construct they call the **work companion**: someone who works alongside you with a shared focus on work but without the obligations of family, friendship, or a common employer. What makes the relationship valuable, on their account, is exactly that absence. Because neither party owes the other anything, members can choose moment to moment between socially engaging and working in parallel, and they extract both personal and professional value from that interaction flexibility; where a family, friendship, or employment tie *is* present, obligations rigidify the interaction and the value falls, which the authors treat as the construct's boundary condition. Space managers matter as curators of the conditions under which companions form. The paper is qualitative and builds theory rather than testing it, but it sits naturally beside the inventor results above. Pennington and Shaver show that proximity outside the firm produces collaboration inside it; Hymer and coauthors describe the micro-relationship through which proximity among strangers does its work, and why a firm cannot simply manufacture it by seating its own employees together. (The published abstract was the only part of the paper accessible when this was written.) Proximity can also be priced. @catalini2020travel move the question from where collaborators live to what it costs them to meet. They build a simple framework in which travel costs shape both whether scientists collaborate at all and which kinds of project get developed locally rather than over distance, then test it against the entry of new low-cost airline routes, a quasi-experiment that lowers the cost of a face-to-face meeting between two cities without changing anything about the science in either. After a low-cost carrier enters, collaborations between the newly connected locations rise by between 0.3 and 1.1 times, a result that survives multiple falsification tests. The gain accrues disproportionately to high-quality scientists otherwise embedded in weaker local environments, which is to say the people for whom the local collaboration pool was the binding constraint. Lower travel costs also change the *kind* of project undertaken, and that is the part with consequences for @sec-innovation-measure: a friction does not simply scale collaboration up or down, it selects which collaborations happen, so a count of coauthored patents is a function of the cost of meeting as much as of the willingness to work together. Read beside the residential result, the two papers bracket the geography of collaboration at both ends, kilometers between homes in one town and airfares between cities, and both find that the physical cost of an encounter shapes an output the firm books as intellectual. ### Dominance, Radicalness, and the Competition–Innovation Curve Who produces *radical* innovation—and who profits from it? @sorescu2003sources find that **dominant** firms introduce *fewer* radical innovations than non-dominant firms, that the financial rewards to radical innovation vary enormously across firms and are tied to the resource base, and that firms with deeper marketing and technology support and broader product portfolios extract more value from the radical innovations they do produce. The relationship between competition and innovation is itself non-monotonic: @aghion2005 establish an **inverted-U**, in which innovation is highest at intermediate product-market competition—too little competition removes the spur to innovate, too much removes the rents that reward it. The contrast between dominant and entrant innovators is sharpened by what happens to a firm's innovation *after* it goes public. @Wies_2015 show that following an initial public offering (IPO), firms raise their innovation *levels*—they innovate more—but the innovations become *less risky*, with fewer breakthroughs, as the discipline of public markets tilts the portfolio toward incremental safety. This post-IPO retreat from radicalness is the empirical hinge connecting the organizational and financial halves of the chapter. ## Innovation and Firm Value Innovation is ultimately an intangible asset, and capital markets price it. The marketing–finance literature—developed in full in @sec-marketing-finance—asks how investors value innovation activity and treats the question with event-study and asset-pricing machinery rather than survey scales. ### How Markets Price New-Product Activity @srinivasan2009a provide the foundational empirical link between product innovation, marketing investment, and stock returns. Their headline magnitudes are striking and worth stating precisely: investors react far more favorably to **pioneering** innovations than to minor updates—on the order of *seven times* greater—and the advertising support behind pioneering innovations is roughly *nine times* more effective in moving returns. Perceived product quality raises returns, while price promotions *lower* them, plausibly because a promotion signals weak underlying demand. The asymmetry between pioneering and incremental innovation is the financial counterpart to the radical-versus-incremental distinction in @sorescu2003sources. The effect of innovation on sales is itself conditioned by brand assets. @slotegraaf2008 show that the permanent and cumulative sales effects of product introductions are larger for brands with higher equity and more frequent releases, while lower-equity brands benefit *more* from each individual introduction—a substitution between brand stock and product flow. Collaboration timing also moves markets: @wu2015sleeping analyze 831 announcements of **horizontal collaborations** (partnering with competitors for NPD) over twelve years and find that markets react *positively* to collaboration at the *initiation* phase but *negatively* during development and commercialization, with the new product's innovativeness and the partner's relative strengths providing asymmetric moderation. ### Innovation Signaling at the IPO Innovation is informative precisely when information is scarcest—at the IPO, when outside investors know least about firm quality. @cao2022express show that firms deploy their **innovation potential** as a credible quality signal at IPO: innovation potential is positively associated with the IPO's initial value and first-day returns and negatively associated with the extent of insider share sales. The components differ in what they signal—patents weigh most heavily on insider selling, while preannouncements move first-day returns most—consistent with a signaling logic in which costlier, harder-to-fake signals (granted patents) carry the most weight where credibility matters most. ### Sustaining Innovation After the IPO The post-IPO innovation decline documented by @Wies_2015 raises the question of what can arrest it. @wu2024innovation examine the role of **AI analytics** in sustaining post-IPO innovation, analyzing patent data from over 1,000 publicly traded firms. Firms that acquire AI-analytics capabilities after their IPO suffer a *smaller* decline in innovation quality, with the effect concentrated in machine-learning capabilities specifically. The mechanism is **recombination**: sustained innovation is driven by the ability to recombine existing technologies into new ones—exactly the backward-citation logic of @sec-innovation-measure—and AI analytics supports that recombination. It mitigates two of the three classic barriers to post-IPO innovation—short-term financial pressure and disclosure requirements (with the disclosure benefit largest for firms with long product cycles)—while doing little for managerial-incentive problems. The broader lesson is that *technology* is itself an input into the production of innovation, and that firms and investors can partially offset the predictable post-IPO innovation slump by investing in it. ## Patent Value from Stock-Market Signals {#sec-innovation-kpss} Forward citations measure a patent's influence on later technology. They do not measure what the patent is worth to the firm that owns it, and @sec-innovation-measure ended on that gap: citations accrue for years after the grant and cannot recover what an investor could have seen at the time. @kogan2017technological (KPSS) proposed a measure that fills it. When the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) announces a grant, the owner's stock price moves. Part of the move is news about the patent and part is everything else that happened that week. KPSS filter the return through a simple statistical model and turn it into a dollar value for every patent granted to a U.S. public firm since 1926. The resulting file is public and updated every year, and it has become the default measure of patent value in finance, economics, and strategy. This section covers the estimator, shows how to run it on real stock returns, and reports what the public file contains. It then turns to @arora2026revisiting, who show that the filter that makes KPSS values precise also builds in a specific kind of measurement error. Their result splits the uses of the measure in two. KPSS values work as a right-hand-side variable. As a dependent variable in a comparison of two groups of patents they are internally inconsistent and biased toward finding no difference, and the section implements the two alternatives they propose. ### The KPSS Estimator {#sec-innovation-kpss-estimator} Let $\xi_j$ be the dollar value of patent $j$ to its owner, and let $\pi$ be the market's prior probability that the application succeeds. On the grant day the market learns only that the application succeeded, so the change in firm value is $$ \Delta V_j = (1 - \pi)\,\xi_j . $$ {#eq-kpss-grant} KPSS measure the reaction with the firm's idiosyncratic return $R_j$, the firm's return minus the market's, compounded over the three trading days $[t, t+2]$ from the grant date (trading volume rises over those days and then settles). The return is split into the patent's value as a fraction of market capitalization, $v_j$, and unrelated news, $\varepsilon_j$: $$ R_j = v_j + \varepsilon_j, \qquad v_j \sim N^{+}\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{v,ft}\right), \qquad \varepsilon_j \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\varepsilon,ft}\right). $$ {#eq-kpss-decomp} The value is truncated at zero because a granted patent cannot destroy value, while the noise can take either sign. Under these assumptions the best prediction of $v_j$ given the observed return is the mean of a truncated normal, $$ E[v_j \mid R_j] = \delta R_j + \sqrt{\delta}\,\sigma_{\varepsilon,ft}\, \frac{\phi\!\left(-\sqrt{\delta}\,R_j/\sigma_{\varepsilon,ft}\right)} {1 - \Phi\!\left(-\sqrt{\delta}\,R_j/\sigma_{\varepsilon,ft}\right)}, \qquad \delta = \frac{\sigma^2_{v,ft}}{\sigma^2_{v,ft} + \sigma^2_{\varepsilon,ft}}, $$ {#eq-kpss-filter} which is increasing and convex in $R_j$. A large negative return maps to a value near zero, and a large positive return maps to roughly $\delta R_j$. The signal-to-noise ratio $\delta$ controls how much of the return is believed. Two parameters are needed. KPSS hold $\delta$ fixed across firms and years, which lets both variances move freely as long as they move in proportion, and estimate it from the extra volatility on grant days: $$ \log R_{fd}^2 = \gamma\, I_{fd} + c' Z_{fd} + u_{fd}, \qquad \hat\delta = 1 - e^{-\hat\gamma}, $$ {#eq-kpss-gamma} where $I_{fd}$ marks grant days and $Z_{fd}$ holds firm-by-year and day-of-week fixed effects. The published estimate is $\hat\gamma = 0.0146$, so $\hat\delta \approx 0.0145$ [@kogan2012technologicalwp]. Only about 1.5% of the variance of a grant-week return is patent news, which is why filtering matters. The noise variance comes from realized volatility. If $\sigma^2_{ft}$ is the firm-year mean of squared daily idiosyncratic returns and $d_{ft}$ the share of trading days that are grant days, then $$ \sigma^2_{\varepsilon,ft} = \frac{3\,\sigma^2_{ft}}{1 + 3\,d_{ft}\left(e^{\hat\gamma} - 1\right)} . $$ {#eq-kpss-noise} Finally the filtered return is scaled to dollars with the market capitalization $M_j$ on the day before the grant, divided equally among the $N_j$ patents the firm received that day, and grossed up for the anticipated part of the news: $$ \xi_j = \frac{1}{1 - \pi}\,\frac{1}{N_j}\,E[v_j \mid R_j]\,M_j . $$ {#eq-kpss-value} KPSS set $\pi = 0.56$, the average grant rate for 1991–2001 applications, which multiplies values by about 2.27. @fig-kpss-pipeline lays out the steps. ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-kpss-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "The KPSS estimator. Every patent a firm receives on a given day gets the same value, since the day's filtered return is simply divided by $N_j$. And the value is a conditional expectation, a prediction of $v_j$ given a noisy signal, not $v_j$ itself. KPSS validate the measure in three ways. Case studies line up with it: an Amazon patent on using shopping-cart contents to generate recommendations, granted in November 2001, was followed by a 34% rise in the stock over two days, while an IBM patent on reserving airplane restrooms drew a slightly negative return despite a citation count in the top fifth of its cohort [@kogan2012technologicalwp]. Value rises with forward citations, and placebo estimates with grant dates reassigned at random within the year center on zero. At the firm level, summing values into an innovation measure predicts the firm's later growth in profits, output, capital, and employment, predicts slower growth at competitors, and in aggregate tracks medium-run swings in productivity [@kogan2017technological]. The median patent is worth about \$3.2 million in 1982 dollars. ### A Toolkit in R {#sec-innovation-kpss-toolkit} The estimator fits in three functions. `kpss_filter()` is @eq-kpss-filter, written with the log inverse Mills ratio so it stays finite for large negative returns. `kpss_sigma_eps()` is @eq-kpss-noise. `gkpss_filter()` is the two-signal generalization derived in @sec-innovation-kpss-groups. The chunk also checks the closed forms against brute-force numerical integration of the posterior. The generalized filter agrees to five decimals and collapses to the KPSS filter when the second signal vanishes. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # E[x | r]: KPSS filter. x ~ N+(0, sx^2), eps ~ N(0, se^2), r = x + eps, # delta = sx^2 / (sx^2 + se^2) kpss_filter <- function(r, delta, sigma_eps) { z <- -sqrt(delta) * r / sigma_eps mills <- exp(dnorm(z, log = TRUE) - pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)) delta * r + sqrt(delta) * sigma_eps * mills } # Noise s.d. over a `window`-day event window, from the firm-year mean squared daily # idiosyncratic return (s2) and the share of trading days that are grant days. kpss_sigma_eps <- function(s2, grant_share, gamma, window = 3) { sqrt(window * s2 / (1 + window * grant_share * (exp(gamma) - 1))) } # Generalized filter: E[x1 | r] when r = x1 + x2 + eps, with x1 ~ N+(0, (theta1*se)^2), # x2 ~ N+(0, (theta2*se)^2), eps ~ N(0, se^2). Swap theta1/theta2 to get E[x2 | r]. gkpss_filter <- function(r, theta1, theta2, sigma_eps) { q <- sqrt(1 + theta1^2 + theta2^2) s <- sigma_eps * q w1 <- s * sqrt(1 + theta2^2) / theta1 w2 <- s * sqrt(1 + theta1^2) / theta2 l1 <- theta2 / theta1 * q l2 <- theta1 / theta2 * q num <- 2 * (1 + theta2^2) * sigma_eps^2 / w1 * dnorm(r / w1) * pnorm(l1 * r / w1) - 2 * theta1^2 * sigma_eps^2 / w2 * dnorm(r / w2) * pnorm(l2 * r / w2) owen <- function(h, a) vapply(h, function(hh) sn::T.Owen(hh, a), numeric(1)) den <- pnorm(r / w1) - 2 * owen(r / w1, l1) + pnorm(r / w2) - 2 * owen(r / w2, l2) theta1^2 / q^2 * r + num / den } # Check both filters against brute-force numerical integration brute <- function(r, s1, s2, se) { t <- sqrt(s2^2 + se^2) fz <- function(z) 2 / t * dnorm(z / t) * pnorm(s2 / se * z / t) # density of x2 + eps f1 <- function(v) 2 / s1 * dnorm(v / s1) integrate(function(v) v * f1(v) * fz(r - v), 0, Inf)$value / integrate(function(v) f1(v) * fz(r - v), 0, Inf)$value } chk <- data.frame(r = c(-2, 0, 1, 2.5)) chk$closed_form <- gkpss_filter(chk$r, 0.4, 0.25, 1) chk$numerical <- sapply(chk$r, brute, s1 = 0.4, s2 = 0.25, se = 1) chk$kpss_limit <- gkpss_filter(chk$r, 0.4, 1e-4, 1) # theta2 -> 0 ... chk$kpss <- kpss_filter(chk$r, 0.4^2 / (1 + 0.4^2), 1) # ... collapses to KPSS round(chk, 5) #> r closed_form numerical kpss_limit kpss #> 1 -2.0 0.21081 0.21081 0.21557 0.21557 #> 2 0.0 0.28723 0.28723 0.29632 0.29633 #> 3 1.0 0.33983 0.33983 0.35239 0.35239 #> 4 2.5 0.44187 0.44187 0.46175 0.46176 ``` ::: ### Running KPSS on Real Returns {#sec-innovation-kpss-pipeline} The pipeline below runs the estimator from scratch on public prices. It downloads daily prices for a firm and for an S&P 500 index fund (a stand-in for the CRSP value-weighted market), builds three-day idiosyncratic returns, estimates the noise variance from trailing 52-week volatility as the current KPSS release does, and applies the filter on each grant day. Daily prices. Patents in a bundle share one value by construction, so they cannot be independent observations. ### What the Filter Does to Measurement Error {#sec-innovation-kpss-error} @arora2026revisiting begin from the fact that a KPSS value is a conditional expectation. Write the true value as $x$ and the KPSS value as $E[x \mid r]$, with measurement error $\omega = E[x \mid r] - x$. Three properties follow: $$ E[\omega] = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\!\left(E[x \mid r]\right) < \operatorname{Var}(x), \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\omega, x) < 0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\omega, E[x \mid r]\right) = 0 . $$ {#eq-kpss-error} The mean is right because of iterated expectations. The variance is too small because of the law of total variance: the variance of a prediction is the variance of the truth minus the variance it leaves unexplained. The error is negatively correlated with the truth: the filter shrinks every value toward the mean, so it undervalues good patents and overvalues bad ones. The error is uncorrelated with the KPSS value itself, which is the defining property of a prediction. In the econometric vocabulary, this is Berkson error rather than classical error, and the two have opposite consequences in a regression. When KPSS is the regressor in $y = \alpha + \beta x + \eta$, substituting $E[x \mid r]$ for $x$ puts $-\beta\omega$ in the error term, and that term is uncorrelated with the regressor, so OLS is unbiased. The raw return $r$ has classical error and is attenuated toward zero by the factor $\operatorname{Var}(x)/\operatorname{Var}(r)$, which at KPSS signal-to-noise levels is close to zero. When KPSS is the dependent variable in a comparison of groups the logic reverses. Shrinkage toward a common mean pulls group means toward each other. @tbl-kpss-sim-error checks each claim by simulation, with a signal-to-noise ratio higher than the empirical one so that the effects are visible in 100,000 draws. KPSS values have the right mean but less than 5% of the true variance. The regression slope on KPSS values is 1.99 against a truth of 2, while the slope on raw returns is 0.08. In the group comparison the reversal appears: KPSS recovers 7% of a true gap that raw returns recover in full. @fig-kpss-compression shows the shrinkage. ::: {#tbl-kpss-sim-error .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Simulated properties of KPSS values (theta = 0.35, 100,000 patents). In the simulation, with $\delta$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon$ known, the understatement is modest: the Monte Carlo standard deviation of the slope is 0.351 against an average OLS standard error of 0.329. In real data two larger problems come first. $\gamma$ and $\sigma_\varepsilon$ are estimated, and values are shared within bundles, which the citation regression above showed can understate standard errors several-fold. A firm-level block bootstrap that re-runs the whole pipeline, from the $\gamma$ regression to the filter, handles all three at once. ### Comparing Patent Groups: Generalized KPSS and Unfiltered Returns {#sec-innovation-kpss-groups} Much of the strategy and innovation literature uses KPSS values as an outcome: are patents from larger teams, science-based patents, or patents from vertically integrated firms worth more? @arora2026revisiting show that the question cannot be answered from KPSS values as published. The estimator imposes one signal-to-noise ratio, which means every patent a firm receives in a year is drawn from the same value distribution. A test of whether two groups differ in mean value is therefore a test of a difference the estimator assumed away. If the groups do differ, the shared $\delta$ sits between the two true ratios, so the high-value group is shrunk too hard and the low-value group not hard enough, and the estimated gap is biased toward zero. On days when a firm receives patents of both types the problem is sharper. The return then carries two signals, the filter in @eq-kpss-filter no longer applies, and equal splitting forces the measured within-day gap to zero. The first remedy keeps the filter but lets each group have its own distribution. Write $\theta_s = \sigma_{x_s}/\sigma_\varepsilon$ and $\theta_n = \sigma_{x_n}/\sigma_\varepsilon$ for the two groups (S and N). The ratios come from a volatility regression with one dummy per day type, $$ \log R_{fd}^2 = \gamma_s I^{S}_{fd} + \gamma_n I^{N\text{-only}}_{fd} + c' Z_{fd} + \nu_{fd}, \qquad \theta_k^2 = e^{\gamma_k} - 1, $$ {#eq-kpss-two-gamma} and the noise variance from the volatility identity with both shares of grant days. On days with only one type, the KPSS filter applies with that type's $\delta_k$. On mixed days the return is $r = x_s + x_n + \varepsilon$, and the posterior mean of the S component, derived with the two-tier stochastic-frontier algebra of @papadopoulos2015halfnormal, is $$ E[x_s \mid r] = \frac{\theta_s^2}{1 + \theta_s^2 + \theta_n^2}\, r + \frac{\dfrac{2(1+\theta_n^2)\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\omega_1}\,\phi\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_1}\right)\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{\lambda_1 r}{\omega_1}\right) - \dfrac{2\theta_s^2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\omega_2}\,\phi\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_2}\right)\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{\lambda_2 r}{\omega_2}\right)} {\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_1}\right) - 2T\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_1}, \lambda_1\right) + \Phi\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_2}\right) - 2T\!\left(\dfrac{r}{\omega_2}, \lambda_2\right)}, $$ {#eq-kpss-two-signal} where $s = \sigma_\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\theta_s^2+\theta_n^2}$, $\omega_1 = s\sqrt{1+\theta_n^2}/\theta_s$, $\omega_2 = s\sqrt{1+\theta_s^2}/\theta_n$, $\lambda_1 = (\theta_n/\theta_s)\sqrt{1+\theta_s^2+\theta_n^2}$, $\lambda_2 = (\theta_s/\theta_n)\sqrt{1+\theta_s^2+\theta_n^2}$, and $T(h, a)$ is Owen's T function. `gkpss_filter()` implements it, and the check in @sec-innovation-kpss-toolkit confirms it against numerical integration. The method needs days on which one type is granted without the other, since those days identify the two ratios. It handles exactly two groups, so continuous characteristics must be split. And a patent's value now depends on which partition the researcher chose. The second remedy drops the filter. Regress the idiosyncratic event return on an indicator for any grant and an indicator for a grant of the group of interest, with firm and date fixed effects and controls for firm size and the number of patents, and compare the coefficients. Unfiltered returns are consistent with any difference in group means and simple to compute, but they are noisy and cannot separate two types granted on the same day. @tbl-kpss-sim-groups runs all of these on a simulated panel of 400 firms over 2,500 trading days, in which S patents carry a larger value scale than N patents and 2.5% of days are mixed. KPSS recovers 2% of the true gap. Unfiltered returns recover 89%. The generalized estimator, with the any-S dummy specified as in @arora2026revisiting, overshoots to 126%: mixed days enter the S dummy, the second signal on those days inflates $\hat\gamma_s$, and an inflated $\theta_s$ exaggerates the S values. A small refinement fixes it. Identify each $\theta$ from pure days only and give mixed days their own dummy, which brings the estimate to 97% of the truth. Across three further seeds the any-S version ranged from 118% to 134% and the pure-day version from 82% to 100%. @arora2026revisiting report a milder overshoot in their own simulation (a gap of 0.0447 against a true 0.04) and attribute it to noise in estimating the parameters. The pure-day specification is our modification, not theirs, and is worth reporting alongside the original. ::: {#tbl-kpss-sim-groups .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Estimated difference in mean patent value between two groups (S minus N) in a simulated panel of 400 firms and 2,500 trading days, with theta_S = 0.30, theta_N = 0.18, 7.5% S-only days, 7.5% N-only days, and 2.5% mixed days. Values are fractions of firm value.'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(data.table); library(fixest) set.seed(33056) nF <- 400; nD <- 2500 # 400 firms x 2,500 trading days th_s <- 0.30; th_n <- 0.18 # S patents carry more value per unit of noise p <- data.table(firm = rep(seq_len(nF), each = nD)) p[, sig := rep(runif(nF, 0.01, 0.03), each = nD)] # firm-specific return noise u <- runif(nrow(p)) # day mix: 7.5% S-only, 7.5% N-only, 2.5% mixed p[, `:=`(nS = as.integer(u < 0.025 | (u >= 0.100 & u < 0.175)), nN = as.integer(u < 0.100))] p[, xs := nS * abs(rnorm(.N, 0, th_s * sig))] p[, xn := nN * abs(rnorm(.N, 0, th_n * sig))] p[, r := xs + xn + rnorm(.N, 0, sig)] p[, `:=`(K = nS + nN, I = as.integer(nS + nN > 0), S_any = nS, N_only = as.integer(nN == 1 & nS == 0), S_only = as.integer(nS == 1 & nN == 0), mixed = as.integer(nS == 1 & nN == 1))] p[, s2 := mean(r^2), by = firm] # realized second moment, one-day window # (1) KPSS: one signal-to-noise ratio, value split equally across the day's patents gam <- coef(feols(log(r^2) ~ I | firm, p))[["I"]] p[, se_k := kpss_sigma_eps(s2, mean(I), gam, window = 1), by = firm] p[I == 1, v_kpss := kpss_filter(r, 1 - exp(-gam), se_k) / K] # (2) Generalized KPSS: separate thetas, two-signal filter on mixed days gen_values <- function(theta_s, theta_n, se_g) { out <- p[, .(nS, nN, r, seg = se_g)] out[nS == 1 & nN == 0, vs := kpss_filter(r, theta_s^2 / (1 + theta_s^2), seg)] out[nN == 1 & nS == 0, vn := kpss_filter(r, theta_n^2 / (1 + theta_n^2), seg)] out[nS == 1 & nN == 1, `:=`(vs = gkpss_filter(r, theta_s, theta_n, seg), vn = gkpss_filter(r, theta_n, theta_s, seg))] out[nS == 1, mean(vs)] - out[nN == 1, mean(vn)] } # (2a) dummies as in Arora et al.: any-S day vs N-only day ga <- coef(feols(log(r^2) ~ S_any + N_only | firm, p)) ts_a <- sqrt(exp(ga[["S_any"]]) - 1); tn_a <- sqrt(exp(ga[["N_only"]]) - 1) se_a <- p[, sqrt(s2[1] / (1 + mean(S_any) * ts_a^2 + mean(N_only) * tn_a^2)), by = firm]$V1 # (2b) refinement: identify each theta from pure days; mixed days get their own dummy gb <- coef(feols(log(r^2) ~ S_only + N_only + mixed | firm, p)) ts_b <- sqrt(exp(gb[["S_only"]]) - 1); tn_b <- sqrt(exp(gb[["N_only"]]) - 1) se_b <- p[, sqrt(s2[1] / (1 + mean(S_only) * ts_b^2 + mean(N_only) * tn_b^2 + mean(mixed) * (ts_b^2 + tn_b^2))), by = firm]$V1 # (3) Unfiltered returns: regress the event return on counts of each patent type ur <- feols(r ~ nS + nN | firm, p, vcov = "hetero") truth <- p[nS == 1, mean(xs)] - p[nN == 1, mean(xn)] res <- data.table( method = c("Truth (simulated values)", "KPSS (one distribution)", "Generalized KPSS, any-S dummy", "Generalized KPSS, pure-day thetas", "Unfiltered returns regression"), gap = c(truth, p[nS == 1, mean(v_kpss)] - p[nN == 1, mean(v_kpss)], gen_values(ts_a, tn_a, rep(se_a, each = nD)), gen_values(ts_b, tn_b, rep(se_b, each = nD)), coef(ur)[["nS"]] - coef(ur)[["nN"]])) res[, pct := round(100 * gap / truth)] res[, gap := sprintf("%.5f", gap)] knitr::kable(res, col.names = c("Estimator", "S minus N mean value", "% of truth")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Estimator |S minus N mean value | % of truth| |:---------------------------------|:--------------------|----------:| |Truth (simulated values) |0.00198 | 100| |KPSS (one distribution) |0.00004 | 2| |Generalized KPSS, any-S dummy |0.00250 | 126| |Generalized KPSS, pure-day thetas |0.00192 | 97| |Unfiltered returns regression |0.00175 | 89| ::: ::: The empirical stakes are large. @arora2026revisiting build a sample of 1,444,649 patents granted 1980–2019 to 4,977 U.S. public firms and compare patent groups three ways. That is the Berkson-versus-classical contrast of @sec-innovation-kpss-error, appearing in data. ### Check the Bundles Before You Compare Groups {#sec-innovation-kpss-bundles} Whether generalized KPSS can work for a given comparison depends on how often the two groups are granted to the same firm on the same day, and the public file answers that before any return data are bought. Section (e) of the public-data chunk runs the check for claim breadth, defining a broad patent as one in the top quartile of distinct CPC subclasses within its main subclass and grant year (13.7% of patents granted 1980–2020). @tbl-kpss-bundles shows the result. | Firm grant days with | Share of firm-days | |---|---| | Narrow patents only | 69.5% | | Both broad and narrow patents (mixed) | 22.3% | | Broad patents only | 8.2% | : Composition of firm grant days for a broad-versus-narrow split, patents granted 1980–2020 in the public KPSS file. {#tbl-kpss-bundles} Mixed days are a minority of days but not of patents. 85.2% of broad patents were granted on a day when the firm also received a narrow one. On those days KPSS assigns broad and narrow patents identical values, so a regression of log value on the broad indicator with firm-by-grant-day fixed effects returns exactly zero. With firm-by-year fixed effects and controls for bundle size the estimate is 0.0003 (s.e. 0.0005). That null cannot tell us whether breadth is unpriced. It is what KPSS produces whether breadth matters or not. The 8.2% of broad-only days are what a generalized estimate or a returns regression would have to work with. The proportions are close to those in @arora2026revisiting, whose mixed-day shares are 22.5% for team size, 22.1% for science reliance, and 13.5% for offshoring. ### Choosing a Stock-Market Measure of Patent Value {#sec-innovation-kpss-choose} @tbl-kpss-choose condenses the guidance of @arora2026revisiting into a choice by research question. | Research question | KPSS | Generalized KPSS | Unfiltered returns | |---|---|---|---| | Does patent value predict an outcome? (value as regressor or control) | Use; bootstrap the pipeline, cluster by firm | Rarely needed; estimates change little | Attenuated toward zero by noise | | Do two groups of patents differ in value? (value as outcome) | Do not use: assumes no difference, biased toward zero | Use when enough single-type days exist | Use; simple and consistent but noisy | | Comparisons across firms or industries | Caution: a common $\delta$ makes volatile firms' patents look valuable | Same caution | Same caution | : Which stock-market patent measure fits which question, after @arora2026revisiting. {#tbl-kpss-choose} A few further rules follow from the construction. Compare patents within firms where possible, because a common $\delta$ ties a firm's value scale to its volatility and a common $\pi$ ignores differences in grant rates. Report results under both alternatives for a group comparison, since they fail in different ways and agreement between them is the strongest evidence available. Remember that the measure prices the patent plus the information its grant conveys, including option value, so it will differ from retrospective survey valuations. And treat values in a bundle as one observation of the firm-day, not $N$ independent patents. The machinery is not specific to patents. It turns any recurring, dated, partly anticipated event into a value per event: product launches, trademark registrations, regulatory approvals, or contract awards. @sec-marketing-finance develops the event study it rests on. For marketing researchers it offers a way to value individual innovations when sales data are missing or arrive years late. ## Key Takeaways - Diffusion is the formal backbone of innovation forecasting. The **Bass model** (@eq-04-bass-hazard, @eq-bass-cumulative) decomposes adoption into innovation ($p$) and imitation ($q$); its parameters are weakly identified before the sales peak, and successive-generation extensions [@Chandrasekaran_2020] are needed when substitution, not saturation, drives an incumbent's decline. - Diffusion often turns on a **supply-side** adoption decision by local merchants, not only on consumer contagion. @xu2026food show that local news coverage causes restaurants and stores to adopt plant-based meat, identifying the effect from quasi-random county-quarter news production across topics (@sec-innovation-news-diffusion); the effect is larger in liberal-leaning counties, so a national average masks a politically sorted map. - Patent **citations** are the field's default innovation measure: backward citations proxy (inverse) novelty and are available *ex ante*, while forward citations proxy importance but accrue *ex post* and require truncation corrections (@tbl-citations). Citations observe only one channel of a patent's value. Serendipitous inventions score lower than planned ones on technological impact, commercialization, and blocking but higher on licensing, so their value is captured outside the firm that made them (@sec-innovation-serendipity) [@grimpe2026accidents]. - NPD outcomes are **contingent**—on the information environment [@moorman1999contingency], team structure [@sethi2001cross; @slotegraaf2011product], and latent firm heterogeneity [@grewal2013environments]—so average effects mislead. Even a team's response to failure is contingent: flat teams recruit high-status members after a setback and perform better for it, while steep teams do not (@fig-innovation-flattest) [@zhong2026flattest]. - Customers invent uses the firm did not design for, and product attributes shape which ones they find. Across 1,925 IKEA hacks, modularity raises the likelihood of new functions (more so with components compatible across product lines, less so with esthetic variants), while visual simplicity raises the likelihood of new functionalities [@lim2026exaptation]; see @sec-innovation-exaptation. - Acquisitions help innovation only under resource **complementarity** [@king2008performance; @mishra2013building], reconciling the otherwise-negative average effect [@hitt1991]; competition and innovation trace an inverted-U [@aghion2005]. - External **scientific** knowledge is not free for the taking. Holding the science itself fixed with *paper twins*, academic findings enter corporate patents along interpersonal ties within two degrees of separation, and only for inventors who are still active in research and whose expertise matches what they are absorbing— absorptive capacity at the individual level [@arts2026harnessing]. Firms also learn at conferences, identified with direct flights as an instrument for attendance [@baruffaldi2024like]. - Some organizational determinants are not chosen. Where a firm's inventors *live* predicts who patents together: each kilometer between two coworkers' homes lowers their odds of coinventing by about 0.3%, the effect survives homophily controls and a within-pair mover test, and it operates only within same-gender pairs [@pennington2026residential]. - Generative AI reshapes the open-source crowd itself. GitHub Copilot raises merged contributions per project by 5.9% but lengthens merge time by 8% through more code discussion, and tilts contribution toward core developers and away from the peripheral volunteers whose knowledge is what makes openness pay [@song2026copilot; @singh2026opensource]. - Markets price innovation asymmetrically—pioneering innovations earn roughly seven times the reaction of incremental ones [@srinivasan2009a]—and the post-IPO retreat from radical innovation [@Wies_2015] can be partly offset by technology investment [@wu2024innovation]. The valuation machinery is developed in @sec-marketing-finance. - The stock-market reaction to a patent grant, filtered through a truncated-normal signal model, gives a dollar value for each patent [@kogan2017technological]; the pipeline in @sec-innovation-kpss-pipeline reproduces the published values from public prices. Because the filter is a conditional expectation, its error is Berkson-type: KPSS values are unbiased as a regressor but compress group differences toward zero as an outcome, so comparisons of patent groups need the generalized two-signal estimator or unfiltered returns [@arora2026revisiting] (@tbl-kpss-choose). - **Generative AI is not one lever at the front end.** Used to concretize a concept, visual support cuts ideator effort but yields ideas 18% less creative than the more effortful textual support [@gordetzki2026ideation]; used to generate concepts, an LLM raises average purchase intent and is seven times likelier to produce a top-decile idea while producing **less novel and less diverse sets**, a shortfall that recurs across prior LLM creativity studies and is recovered by pooling vendors, chain-of-thought and persona prompting, creative agents, or sheer scale [@terwiesch2026creativity]. Because a tournament consumes the maximum of a pool rather than its mean, set-level coverage is the metric to report (@sec-innovation-llm-diversity).
